worst_places.before: A common middle-level mistake is rebuilding the application separately for each environment (staging, production) — different builds can pick up different dependency versions or environment-baked config, so what passed staging isn't provably the same artifact running in production.
worst_places.after: 'Build once, promote everywhere' means you build a single immutable artifact — a Docker image tagged by commit SHA, or a versioned package — exactly once, then move that same artifact through staging and production, changing only runtime configuration. Rebuilding per environment is the common mistake it prevents: two builds can pick up different dependency versions or different environment-baked config, so what passed staging is not provably the artifact running in production.

worst_places.after:
The cost is running double the infrastructure for as long as both environments exist.

That "all traffic at once" switch is what separates blue-green from canary. A canary deploy sends only a small percentage of traffic to the new version and grows that share gradually, so a bad release reaches fewer users — a smaller blast radius. Pick canary when limiting that radius matters more than instant rollback, and when you don't want to pay for two full environments. Pick blue-green when you want the simplest possible instant rollback.

patterns: The `**Common pitfall:**` / `**Частая ловушка:**` block is one sentence in 19 of 20 answers, and 95% of the sentences in it are over the word limit in EN (86% in RU) against 54%/33% in the answer bodies. The shape is always the same: 'Doing X — [why it's wrong], [what happens], [what to do instead]' welded together with an em-dash and a semicolon. It is the last thing the reader sees in every single card, and it is the hardest sentence in every single card. Splitting these 20 blocks into 3-4 sentences each is the highest-value single edit available in this zone.

Difficulty seam: yes, and it sits at junior→middle, not at middle→senior. Over-limit sentence rate jumps 35% → 64% → 73% in EN and 13% → 49% → 53% in RU; average answer length goes 80 → 153 → 230 words. The five junior answers are genuinely good (short, one idea per sentence, code immediately after the lead) and read like a different, better-edited document than q6-q20. Whatever editing pass produced the junior tier was not applied to the other fifteen.

Russian addresses the reader in two incompatible registers. Questions are «вы» («Как бы вы оптимизировали…», «Объясните…»), while roughly half the answers reply in «ты»-imperatives («Начни», «разбей», «Кэшируй», «профилируй», «держи», «не давай», «ставь», «Храни») and the other half stay neutral. The switch happens inside single cards. Pick one — the neutral «мы»/infinitive form used in q10-q13 works with both.

English technical terms are conjugated as Russian verbs instead of being translated or glossed: «assume'ить», «скоупленные», «ключуется», «митигировали», «матчить», «метрика-based», «межjob-заражения». This is a milder form of the transliteration layer flagged in the cicd-devops *articles* («аутаджи», «дрейнирует») — the bank has none of those specific words, but the same instinct, applied to verbs. Each instance costs the reader a decode step on top of an already long sentence.

Code blocks are the weakest part of a bank whose subject is configuration. q14's block is prose-as-comments in GitLab-CI syntax inside an otherwise GitHub-Actions bank; q3's YAML omits `runs-on` from two of three jobs; q10 invents `kubectl set canary`. Where the examples are real (q7, q13, q15, q19, q20) they are excellent — the problem is concentrated in the answers that most need a concrete anchor.
notes: Verdict is `systemic-refactor` on the strength of three averages at or near 2 (A, B, F) affecting 15 of 20 cards in both locales, not on the C axis — C = 4 here, and leads are the bank's best feature (indirect_leads = 0; q14's «Начни с профилирования» and q18's three-part opener answer before explaining). So the refactor needed is narrow but wide: split long sentences, expand a glossary's worth of abbreviations, unify RU pronoun register. The zone's own subject, CI/CD, is never expanded in either locale — that one line is the cheapest fix on the site. The RU file is easier to read than the EN one on every measure (45% vs 62% over-limit), so EN needs the heavier pass. I did not verify the articles' claim of «Старший нюанс»-style headings here: the bank has none of it, its headings are clean.
